newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE - Stocks' recovery aids flattening.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE - Stocks' recovery aids flattening.

text.p: It was almost as if last Friday never happened.
On Tuesday afternoon, the shape of the U.S. Treasury yield curve looked as it did before Friday's huge stock market selloff sparked a significant steepening.
"As the stock market has rallied most of the way back, the curve has given up the steepening caused by it," said Hussein Malik, Treasury market analyst at J.P. Morgan Securities Inc.
"We gained five basis points on Friday, and we have given that up."
He said the yield curve typically steepens when the stock market sells off sharply.

Over the past eight years, there have been 20 occassions in which the the Dow Jones Industrial Average has fallen more than 100 points, with the two-year note to 30-year-bond spread widening on 16 of those instances, Malik pointed out.

The yield curve started steepening -- albeit slowly -- immediately after this month's three disappointing Treasury quarterly refunding auctions. The two-to-30-year bond spread rose from a low of 56 basis points earlier this month to 68 basis points last week.
But following the 3.0 percent fall in the Dow Industrials on Friday, the curve swelled to 73 basis points, as investors bailed out of stocks in favor of short-term Treasuries.
As a result, bill rates and two-year note yields fell much more sharply than the 30-year.

But, "Fears of (another big) stock market selloff are out of the market," said Scott Graham, co-head government bond trader at Prudential Securities Inc. "The curve should re-align itself toward flatter levels."
Signs of a significant "correction" back to a flatter curve emerged on Tuesday morning when a large hedge fund reportedly unwound a steepening trade and others put on flattening trades.
While the 30-year yield fell to 6.51 percent from 6.52 percent on Monday, the two-year yield rose to 5.84 percent from 5.80 percent.
"We will give back all the steepening when we are all done," said Graham. "The curve has a chance to move 15 basis points to the flattening side."

Graham and other traders said they expected the long end to lead the way, with the shorter end underperforming. Traders noted that at 5.84 percent, 34 basis points over federal funds rate, the short end has little room to move any lower.
Actually, players said, it is a good bet the two-year yield will move higher, as the market sets up and builds in concessions for next week's two- and five-year note auction.

Malik said the curve, from a value perspective, "is steep given the level of rates and expectations of Fed tightening later this year; two-year yields are within 10 basis points of their recent lows, while 30-year yields are still 20 basis points higher than recent lows."
